questions.q: Given console.log("one"); setTimeout(() => console.log("two"), 0); console.log("three");, what is the logged order?
options: one, two, three
one, three, two
two, one, three
three, two, one
questions.explain: setTimeout's callback never runs until all currently running synchronous code finishes, even with a 0ms delay — so 'three' logs before 'two'.

A queue of HTTP requests waiting to be sent
Where JavaScript's synchronous code actually executes, one function frame at a time
A list of all variables currently in scope
questions.explain: The call stack tracks which function is currently running; JavaScript only runs one thing on it at a time.

questions.q: Why do setTimeout and fetch not block the call stack while they wait?
options: They run instantly behind the scenes
They are handed off to Web APIs outside the JS engine, which notify the task queue when finished
JavaScript secretly uses multiple threads for them
They are converted into synchronous code automatically
questions.explain: Web APIs (browser or Node runtime features) do the actual waiting/networking outside the single-threaded JS engine, then queue a callback for later.

questions.q: Given console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); console.log("D");, what prints?
options: A, B, C, D
A, D, B, C
A, D, C, B
D, A, C, B
questions.explain: Synchronous code (A, D) runs first, then the microtask queue (the Promise's C) is fully drained before the macrotask queue (the setTimeout's B) gets a turn.

questions.q: Why can a single very long synchronous loop freeze an entire web page?
options: Loops are disabled by the browser after a few seconds
The loop automatically triggers a page reload
It occupies the only call stack, so the event loop never gets a chance to run any other queued work until it finishes
setTimeout callbacks always run before loops finish
questions.explain: JavaScript is single-threaded — one call stack. A long synchronous task keeps that stack busy, blocking timers, rendering, and event handling until it completes.
